Afghanistan.polity: Post-Hephthalite principalities (including the Nezak of Kapisa) and Western Turkic rulers in Tokharistan; Sasanian frontier near Herat
Afghanistan.summary: After the Hephthalites were destroyed by the Western Turks and Sasanians in the 560s, the land was divided among local principalities. Tokharistan (Bactria) slipped from Sasanian control after 579 and came under Western Turkic power. Buddhism flourished: the colossal Bamiyan Buddhas, generally dated to the 6th–7th centuries, stood in the central mountains, and Xuanzang recorded Buddhist sites while crossing the region around 628–632.

events.t: After 579, battles with the Western Turks cost the Sasanians control of Tokharistan (Bactria).
Turk-backed Hephthalite forces reach Badghis and Herat; the Sasanian general Bahram Chobin defeats them and takes Balkh.
The colossal Bamiyan Buddhas belong to this era; sources date them to roughly the 6th–7th centuries (dating debated).
Xuanzang crosses Tokharistan (c. 628–632), describing its Buddhist monasteries; his account is the earliest text describing the Bamiyan Buddhas.

Pakistan.polity: Kingdom of Sindh ruled from Aror; local rulers in Gandhara and the Punjab
Pakistan.summary: Sindh was ruled from Aror. The later Chachnama, a 13th-century Persian translation of an earlier Arabic history, preserves a local tradition that the Brahman Chach rose against the previous dynasty and founded his own line; its dates are uncertain. Gandhara's great Buddhist age was past, though monasteries such as Takht-i-Bahi remained in use into the 7th century. Multan was known for its ancient Sun Temple.

events.t: Xuanzang passes through the northwest on his way to India, which he reaches by 633.
Around this time, by Chachnama tradition, the Brahman Chach takes power in Sindh; the dating is uncertain.

sources.title: Buddhist Ruins of Takht-i-Bahi and Neighbouring City Remains at Sahr-i-Bahlol

India.polity: Harsha of Kannauj (north), Chalukyas of Badami (Deccan), Pallavas of Kanchi (southeast), Maitrakas of Valabhi (west)
India.summary: After the Gupta collapse, regional dynasties competed. Harsha (r. 606–647) ruled from Thanesar and later Kannauj; his court author Bana wrote the Harshacharita. Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas (r. 610–642) drove him back to the Narmada and fought the Pallava Mahendravarman I. Valabhi under the Maitrakas was a celebrated seat of learning. Xuanzang reached India by 633 and became close to Harsha.

events.t: Shrines to Shiva and Vishnu are cut at Badami, base of the Early Chalukya dynasty.
Harsha is crowned at Thanesar after his elder brother Rajyavardhana is assassinated; the Harsha era begins.
Pulakeshin II begins his Chalukya reign; his early years are taken up by civil war.
Pulakeshin II drives Harsha back to the Narmada, ending his Deccan campaign (date disputed).
Narasimhavarman I succeeds Mahendravarman I as Pallava king; he later avenges Pallava defeats by capturing the Chalukya capital Vatapi.

sources.title: South Asia: South, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Nepal.polity: Licchavi kingdom of the Kathmandu Valley
Nepal.summary: The Kathmandu Valley was ruled by the Licchavi dynasty (c. 450–750), of Indian origin, which used Sanskrit as its court language and issued Indian-style coins. The powerful figure Amshuvarman is associated with the end of Licchavi dominance, but sources disagree on his dates and status. The Harsha era beginning in 606 was long used in Nepal.

events.t: The Harsha era begins; it was long preserved in Nepal for dating.

Bhutan.summary: No written records are known for this land in 570–632, and its political organisation in this period is unknown.

Bangladesh.summary: The western delta formed part of Gauda, whose king Shashanka annexed much of the Ganges valley in the early 7th century and clashed with the Maukharis and Harsha's family. Pundranagara (Mahasthangarh), founded around the 4th–3rd century BCE, remained a centre of monasteries and temples. Samatata in the east was a famous Mahayana Buddhist centre, as Xuanzang's travel account attests.

events.t: Shashanka of Gauda is held responsible for assassinating Rajyavardhana; Harsha allies with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa against him.
Shashanka dies, never defeated by Harsha, whose later eastern campaign meets little resistance.
Xuanzang's travels in India (630s–640s) include Pundravardhana and Samatata, which he describes as thriving religious centres.

sources.title: Cultural Landscape of Mahasthan and Karatoya River (Tentative List)

Sri Lanka.summary: The island was ruled from Anuradhapura by Sinhala kings, including Aggabodhi I and Aggabodhi II, whose reigns are recorded in the Pali chronicle Culavamsa. Its chronology for this period is only approximate. Theravada Buddhist monasteries dominated religious life.

sources.title: Cūlavaṃsa, being the more recent part of the Mahāvaṃsa, translated by Wilhelm Geiger (2 vols., 1929–1930)

Kazakhstan.summary: The steppes belonged to the western branch of the Turkic (Kök Türk) empire, first ruled by Bumin's brother Ishtemi and then by Tardu, under whom it expanded towards Byzantium. Nomadic pastoralism dominated, while Sogdian merchants supplied the Turks with administrators and trade links, persuading the khagan to open contact with Byzantium to sell silk. Tong Yabghu was supreme khagan in the 620s.

events.t: Ishtemi's rule ends and Tardu succeeds him as ruler of the western Turks.
Tardu's reign ends, after the western Turkic realm has expanded to the borders of Byzantium.
A large Western Turkic army, allied with Heraclius against Persia, campaigns in the Caucasus and storms Darband.

sources.title: History of Central Asia: The Middle Ages

Kyrgyzstan.summary: The Chu valley held Suyab (Ak-Beshim, east of modern Bishkek), a town probably founded by Sogdians in the 6th century. The district was densely settled, subject to the Turks, and dotted with trading colonies of Sogdian merchants, while Turkic nomads pastured the surrounding mountains. The Western Turkic khagan Tong Yabghu dominated the region until his assassination.

events.t: Tong Yabghu, khagan of the Western Turks, is assassinated (628 or 630; date disputed).
Xuanzang passes through Suyab, the town's first recorded mention.

sources.title: Khotan ii. History in the Pre-Islamic Period

Tajikistan.polity: Sogdian towns (Panjikant) in the north; Tokharistan principalities in the south under Western Turkic power
Tajikistan.summary: The north lay in Sogdiana, where Panjikant was a prosperous town of merchants and landowners whose houses and two great temples were decorated with murals of deities, feasts and epic tales. The south belonged to upper Tokharistan, formerly Hephthalite and later under Western Turkic control. Caravan trade and irrigated farming sustained the region, and Buddhist monasteries existed in Tokharistan.

events.t: The Hephthalites are destroyed by the Western Turks and Sasanians (c. 563–566), leaving the region to Turkic overlordship.
Panjikant flourishes; its temples and houses bear murals forming the fullest set of 5th–8th-century Sogdian painting.
Xuanzang crosses Tokharistan (c. 628–632), describing its Buddhist monasteries.

sources.title: Buddhism iv. Buddhist Sites in Afghanistan and Central Asia

Turkmenistan.summary: Merv was a major Sasanian city in Khorasan, with a mint and a population of Zoroastrians, Christians and Buddhists; a Buddhist stupa and monastery there are the westernmost excavated Buddhist buildings known. Khorasan faced repeated pressure from the Turks and their Hephthalite allies, and Merv profited from caravan trade.

events.t: Bahram Chobin defeats a Turk-backed Hephthalite invasion of Khorasan that had reached Badghis and Herat.
Bahram Chobin rebels and Hormizd IV is killed; Khosrow II regains the throne in 591 with Byzantine help.
Turkic forces defeat the Armenian general Smbat Bagratuni and raid as far as Ray and Isfahan; Smbat later campaigns against them.

sources.title: Khorasan iii. Historical Geography in the Late Sasanid-Early Islamic Periods

Uzbekistan.polity: Sogdian city-states (Samarkand, Bukhara) under Western Turkic overlordship
Uzbekistan.summary: Sogdiana's city-states, led by Samarkand and Bukhara, were ruled by local kings who sent tribute to China and lived under Turkic overlordship. Sogdian merchants dominated Silk Road trade and gave the Turks their first chancellery language. Most Sogdians were Zoroastrians, though Buddhist monasteries stood at Termez in the south.

events.t: Sogdian merchants persuade the Turkic khagan to open contact with Byzantium to sell Chinese silk (c. 568–575).
Xuanzang passes through Samarkand, noting that the Sogdians were Zoroastrians, then crosses the Iron Gates into Bactria.

sources.title: Buddhism iv. Buddhist Sites in Afghanistan and Central Asia

Mongolia.summary: Mongolia was the centre of the eastern branch of the Turkic Khaganate founded by Bumin in the 550s, ruled first by his son Muhan. Mounted pastoralists ruled a vast tribal confederation, relying on Sogdians for their chancellery, while Sogdian merchants brought Buddhism and Manichaeism. The Eastern Turks fought the Chinese dynasties until 630, when Tang emperor Taizong defeated them and occupied Mongolia.

events.t: Muhan, ruler of the eastern Turkic realm since 553, ends his reign.
The Bugut stele, written in Sogdian, is raised for the dead khagan Taspar, the oldest surviving inscription on Turkic rulers.
Tang emperor Taizong defeats the Eastern Turks and occupies Mongolia.
